lead: A nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) is a finite-state machine that may have zero, one or many moves on the same input symbol. It accepts a string when at least one possible run ends in a final state. This freedom makes NFAs compact for patterns such as “the string contains 01” or “the third symbol from the right is 1”. They are used in text search, lexical analysers and regular-expression engines. The cost is that a run is a specification of allowed choices, not a step-by-step program. A DFA is the deterministic cousin, with exactly one move per symbol.
prereq: You need: 1.2 Deterministic finite automata for the state idea, and 1.3 Transition diagrams, tables and extended transition function for reading a transition table.

blocks.text: In a DFA, δ(q, a) is one state. In an NFA, δ(q, a) is a set of states. The machine may stay in q, move to another state, or have no move at all. That set is the whole difference.
M = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F),  δ: Q × Σ → 2<sup>Q</sup>
blocks.where: Q is the finite set of states; Σ is the input alphabet; q₀ ∈ Q is the start state; F ⊆ Q is the set of final states; δ(q, a) is the set of states the NFA may enter from q on symbol a; 2<sup>Q</sup> is the power set of Q, the set of all subsets of Q.

blocks.text: The power set contains every subset of Q, including Q itself and the empty set. So δ(q, a) = ∅ is a legal entry. It means no move, not an error. A state may also have no outgoing arrow for a symbol.

In a table, every cell is a set. The figure shows q0 looping on 0 and 1 and also having an arrow to q1 on 1. On input 1 from q0 the machine may stay in q0 or jump to q1. That jump is a choice. The next chapter adds ε-moves in 1.5 NFA with epsilon transitions.

A run is a sequence of states s₀, s₁, …, sₙ. Here s₀ = q₀, and for each input symbol aᵢ, the next state sᵢ satisfies sᵢ ∈ δ(sᵢ₋₁, aᵢ). For input w = a₁a₂…aₙ, the NFA accepts w if some run has sₙ ∈ F. One accepting run is enough.
Draw all runs together as a computation tree. The root is q₀. Each level reads one input symbol. A state q at one level gets a child for every state in δ(q, a) at the next level.

items: Put the start state q₀ at the root.
For each input symbol a, give every state q in the current level a child for each state in δ(q, a).
After the last symbol, look at the leaves. Accept if any leaf is in F. Reject if no leaf is in F.

blocks.text: A leaf may have no children when δ(q, a) = ∅. That branch dies. A dead branch does not reject the string by itself, because another branch may still reach a final state. The extended transition function on sets is δ̂(P, a) = ⋃<sub>q ∈ P</sub> δ(q, a), where P is a set of states and ⋃ is set union.

sections.h3: Designing an NFA: make a guess

blocks.text: Nondeterminism is often called perfect guessing. The machine guesses the right moment to jump to a new state. It is a specification of allowed choices, not a program that flips coins. All choices are explored at once in the computation tree.

items: Strings containing 01 over {0, 1}: use q0 for “no 01 yet”, q1 for “saw a 0 waiting for 1”, and q2 final for “saw 01”. Set δ(q0, 0) = {q0, q1}, δ(q0, 1) = {q0}, δ(q1, 1) = {q2}, δ(q2, 0) = δ(q2, 1) = {q2}, and other entries ∅. The move to q1 on 0 guesses that this 0 starts the 01.

Strings ending in ab over {a, b}: q0 loops on a and b; on a it may also go to q1. From q1, b goes to q2 final. Set δ(q0, a) = {q0, q1}, δ(q0, b) = {q0}, δ(q1, b) = {q2}, δ(q1, a) = ∅, δ(q2, ·) = ∅. The jump guesses the last a.

The third symbol from the right is 1: use the figure. q0 loops on 0 and 1, and on 1 it may also jump to q1. Then q1 goes to q2 on any symbol, and q2 goes to q3 final on any symbol. The jump guesses that the current 1 is third from the right. A wrong guess dies; another run may survive.

blocks.text: Some syllabi write “non-deterministic finite automaton”. NFAs are no stronger than DFAs: every NFA language is also a DFA language. The subset construction in 1.6 Equivalence of NFA and DFA proves it. NFAs are often smaller and easier to design.

figure.caption: Each box is the set of states the NFA may be in after another symbol of 0110. The guess adds q1 at the first 1, and after the last 0 the set contains q3, so the string is accepted.

spec.aria: An NFA q0 to q3 where q0 loops on 0 and 1 and guesses into q1 on 1, then 0 or 1 to q2 and q3; below, the state sets {q0}, {q0}, {q0, q1}, {q0, q1, q2}, {q0, q2, q3} while reading 0110.

examples.question: Build an NFA over {0, 1} for L = {w : the third symbol from the right is 1} and trace the set of states on input 0110.
steps: Set the states Q = {q0, q1, q2, q3}, alphabet Σ = {0, 1}, start state q₀ = q0, and final set F = {q3}.
Start the trace with the set {q0}. Read 0: only q0 is active and δ(q0, 0) = {q0}, so the next set is {q0}.
Read the second symbol 1: δ(q0, 1) = {q0, q1}, so the set becomes {q0, q1}.
Read the third symbol 1: from q0 we get {q0, q1}; from q1 we get {q2}. Union: {q0, q1, q2}.
Read the fourth symbol 0: from q0 we get {q0}; from q1 we get {q2}; from q2 we get {q3}. Union: {q0, q2, q3}.
The final set {q0, q2, q3} contains q3, which is in F. So the string is accepted.
examples.answer: The NFA accepts 0110 because q3 is in the final state set {q0, q2, q3}; the third symbol from the right of 0110 is 1.

traps: δ(q, a) is a set. Writing q2 instead of {q2} is wrong, and writing a blank instead of ∅ is wrong.
One failing run does not reject the string. Rejection means no run reaches a final state.
Do not drop the start state. The trace begins with {q₀}, and q₀ may also be final if q₀ ∈ F.
When tracing, take the union over every active state. Forgetting one branch can lose the accepting leaf.
A label “0, 1” on one arrow means two separate transitions, not the single symbol 0,1.

quiz.q: Define an NFA formally. What is the type of δ?
quiz.a: M = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F), where Q is a finite set of states, Σ is the input alphabet, q₀ ∈ Q is the start state, F ⊆ Q is the set of final states, and δ: Q × Σ → 2<sup>Q</sup> maps a state and a symbol to a set of states.

quiz.q: Why is δ(q, a) = ∅ allowed in an NFA but not in a DFA?
quiz.a: In an NFA, δ(q, a) is a set of possible next states. The empty set is a legal subset and means no move on that symbol. In a DFA, δ(q, a) must be exactly one state, so ∅ is not allowed.

quiz.q: For the NFA in the figure, trace the set of states on input 110. Is 110 accepted?
quiz.a: Start {q0}. Read 1: {q0, q1}. Read 1: from q0 {q0, q1}, from q1 {q2}, union {q0, q1, q2}. Read 0: from q0 {q0}, from q1 {q2}, from q2 {q3}, union {q0, q2, q3}. q3 is final, so 110 is accepted.

quiz.q: Draw the computation tree for input 0110 on the NFA from the worked example. Which root-to-leaf path accepts?
quiz.a: Level 0: q0. After 0: q0. After 01: q0 and q1. After 011: q0, q1 and q2. After 0110: q0, q2 and q3. The accepting path is q0 → q0 → q1 → q2 → q3: stay on 0, jump on the first 1, then move on 1 and 0.

quiz.q: Design an NFA over {0, 1} for strings containing 01. Give δ.
quiz.a: Q = {q0, q1, q2}, q₀ = q0, F = {q2}. δ(q0, 0) = {q0, q1}, δ(q0, 1) = {q0}, δ(q1, 1) = {q2}, δ(q2, 0) = δ(q2, 1) = {q2}, and all other entries are ∅.

quiz.q: A student says “this run died, so the NFA rejects the string”. What is wrong with that statement?
quiz.a: An NFA rejects only when no run reaches a final state. One run can die at an empty set while another run continues and accepts. Acceptance needs just one successful run.

quiz.q: Why is nondeterminism called a specification rather than a program?
quiz.a: The transition table lists all allowed choices. It does not say which choice to take at run time. A real deterministic program must simulate all choices, as subset construction does.

beyond: Not for the exam. NFAs are the working core of many regular-expression engines: Thompson construction turns a pattern into an NFA, and subset construction or a lazy simulation runs it. Hardware and software pattern matchers for network intrusion detection often simulate many NFA states at once. Search next for “Thompson construction”, “subset construction” and “Rabin–Scott powerset construction”. These ideas lead to automata-based string matching and to the equivalence proof in the next chapter.
